name: GridFeed Street Cart Vendor All-Weather Stand Rig
description:
The working uniform of someone who runs a food cart at a Circuit-level transit hub or factory gate, assembled for maximum function across a twelve-hour outdoor shift in Meridian's unpredictable acid-rain cycles. The outermost layer is a full-length rubberized apron in deep charcoal with a GridFeed street-brand logo — a stylized fork wrapped in a signal wave — stamped in white across the chest bib. It's not a corponation; GridFeed is a small Circuit-level vendor supply cooperative that sells aprons, cart equipment, and bulk food inputs to independent vendors, and the logo on the apron is a mark of membership, not employment. Beneath the apron is a long-sleeve thermal work shirt in burnt orange with ribbed cuffs, a relaxed collar, and two breast pockets; the left pocket holds a small order stylus and a folded cloth for wiping down surfaces. Trousers are dark navy cargo-cut in a stain-resistant synth-cotton blend, with a wide waistband and a deep front pocket configured to carry a card reader and a personal comm unit simultaneously.

Footwear is the Ashgrove Linework Work Boot in black with a non-slip sole rated for wet and grease-slicked surfaces — essential for anyone working around hot oil and condensation runoff. The head is covered with a tall white cook's cap or, in rain, a waterproof brimmed hat in matching charcoal with the GridFeed logo repeated on the front. Hands cycle between bare (for fine work) and nitrile gloves (for food handling), kept in a side apron pocket in a continuous rotation. The gene-compatible cut of the apron includes a reinforced tail slot at the back lower hem — a wide, finished opening that accommodates a full prehensile tail without bunching or restriction, since enough Circuit-level vendors have geneware modifications that GridFeed built it into their standard apron pattern. The whole rig smells permanently of whatever's on the menu today: chili oil, fermented soy, spiced protein paste, rain-steam.
functionality: Acid-rain and splash protection via rubberized apron, non-slip boot soles for wet and grease surfaces, card reader and comm pocket in trousers, continuous nitrile glove rotation from side pocket, tall cook's cap for food safety compliance, gene-compatible tail slot in apron hem, thermal shirt for cold-shift temperature regulation, stain-resistant trouser fabric
what_it_says: This person feeds the Circuit. They know every factory shift change time within six blocks, they know which workers take their protein hot and which ones want it cold, and they have been standing in the same spot since before the sun came up. The GridFeed apron marks cooperative membership — a small act of collective organizing in a city dominated by corponations. The burnt-orange shirt is personal choice; it's the one place in the uniform where individuality is permitted.
manufacturer: GridFeed Vendor Cooperative (apron, hat); assembled personal components from Circuit market suppliers
price_range: Φ95–Φ160 (cooperative membership includes subsidized apron; personal components purchased separately)
story_hooks: A vendor's cart is the only fixed point of contact for a network of workers passing information between factory floors — orders placed in specific combinations function as coded messages that have been running for eight months without detection.

The GridFeed cooperative's bulk food input supply has been quietly substituted with a cheaper protein analog that isn't cleared for human consumption — vendors are the last line of detection before it reaches customers.

A regular customer hasn't shown up in four days; the vendor knows their order, their shift schedule, and their face well enough to know something is wrong, and the only person who seems to care is wearing a charcoal apron.

physical_description.visual_profile: A practical, weather-hardened street vendor silhouette. Full-length rubberized charcoal apron dominates the visual frame, stamped with GridFeed's white fork-and-signal-wave logo across the chest bib. Burnt orange thermal undershirt visible at collar and cuffs. Navy cargo trousers peek below apron hem. Black work boots anchor the frame. White cook's cap or charcoal rain hat tops the ensemble. Overall impression: utilitarian, functional, Circuit-tier working class.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed and purposefully loose. The apron hangs straight without cinching, allowing full range of motion for food prep and cart operation. Thermal shirt has easy shoulder room; cargo trousers sit high on the waist with a generous cut through the thigh. Boots are sturdy and slightly broken-in. Everything designed for twelve-hour outdoor shifts, not aesthetics.
physical_description.primary_material: Rubberized synthetic rubber (apron); merino-blend thermal knit (undershirt); synth-cotton stain-resistant blend (trousers); vulcanized rubber and black leather (boots); nitrile for gloves (consumable); cotton-poly blend (cook's cap and rain hat)
physical_description.texture: Apron has a smooth, slightly tacky rubberized finish that sheds grease and condensation. Thermal shirt is soft ribbed knit with subtle texture at cuffs and collar. Cargo trousers have a matte, utilitarian weave. Boots are scuffed and broken in, with tread-worn rubber soles.
physical_description.color_scheme: Dominant charcoal (apron, rain hat). Bright white (GridFeed logo, cook's cap). Burnt orange (thermal undershirt). Navy (cargo trousers). Black (boots). Secondary grease and food stains (organic accumulation) visible on apron bib and pocket edges.
physical_description.closures: Apron: ties at neck and waist (adjustable fabric straps). Thermal shirt: open collar, no buttons. Trousers: standard synthetic zipper fly with wide fabric waistband. Boots: lace-up with friction-fit heel. Rain hat: chin strap with magnetic snap. Glove pocket: friction-fit elastic opening.
distinctive_features: Reinforced tail slot at apron back hem — finished opening accommodating prehensile geneware without restriction
GridFeed logo stamped in white across chest bib (membership marker, not employment)
Integrated pocket configuration on apron: left side holds order stylus and cleaning cloth, right side holds rotating nitrile gloves
Front cargo trousers pocket engineered for simultaneous card reader and personal comm unit carry
Breast pockets on thermal shirt (left pocket typically occupied by stylus, right for notes or comms)
Non-slip sole on Ashgrove Linework boots — rated for grease and wet surfaces
Repeating GridFeed logo on rain hat brim
Permanent food-oil and fermented-soy patina on apron fabric from daily wear
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3–4 working class. GridFeed cooperative membership signals a formalized vendor operation (Tier 3 stability), but the assembled, repair-ready nature of components and the weathering suggest Circuit-level economy rather than corpo infrastructure.
physical_description.cultural_context: Street vendor, food cart operator, Circuit economy worker. Wearing this marks someone as functionally independent — not employed by a mega-corp, but part of a local cooperative network. The tail slot signals acceptance and normalization of geneware modification in working-class spaces. This is the uniform of someone who feeds the GLMZ's transit hubs, factory gates, and informal markets.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in and perpetually weathered. The apron will show stains from the day's menu (oil residue, soy-paste splatters, rain streaks), but the rubberized surface keeps it from absorbing odors permanently. Boots scuffed and creased from constant movement. Thermal shirt collar slightly frayed at the edges. Overall: functional, worn, honest.
